description: We are DIVERGENT, participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We use NASA Earth data and statistical analysis to explore environmental trends, compare regions, and identify significant changes. We welcome members interested in AI, data science, web development, and Earth science.
summary: Earth System Trend Explorer is a free web app that turns decades of NASA Earth observation data into clear, honest answers about how our planet is changing. A user picks an Earth system (climate, biosphere, land surface, cryosphere or ocean), one of 21 variables, a region and a season, and the app answers six questions: what is changing, where, how much, when the major change happened, whether it is statistically significant, and how reliable the result is. It reads NASA POWER (MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, CERES) live and uses bundled samples of NASA GISTEMP, MODIS, MUR SST and the NSIDC Sea Ice Index. Every result comes from transparent statistics (autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope, change-point tests), is checked against an independent dataset, and carries a "How sure are we?" confidence rating. Research Mode shows every statistic for scientists; Everyday Mode explains the same result in plain language for farmers, students and communities, with a live NASA GIBS satellite map, mobile-first design and shareable results. This matters because a trend is only useful when people can trust it: our tool separates real, significant change from noise and shows its uncertainty, helping communities in climate-vulnerable places like Bangladesh plan with evidence.
details:
**What it does**

Earth System Trend Explorer helps anyone find out whether a part of the Earth system is really changing, and how sure we can be. The user picks an Earth system (Climate, Biosphere, Land Surface, Cryosphere or Ocean), one of 21 variables, a region and a time period. Regions include all of Bangladesh, its eight divisions, the Sundarbans, the Eastern and Central Himalaya, the Northern and Central Bay of Bengal, the Arctic Ocean, or any point tapped on the map. Seasons can be the whole year, pre-monsoon, monsoon, post-monsoon, winter or any single month.

The app then answers six questions: What is changing? Where is it changing (a grid-cell map of change)? How much (Sen's slope per decade with a 95% interval)? When did the major change happen (change point)? Is it significant (autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall)? How reliable is it (data coverage, record length and agreement with an independent dataset)?

Every result is told twice: in Research Mode with every statistic, and in Everyday Mode in plain language.

**How it works**

The app runs fully in the browser: no server, no login, no install. It reads NASA POWER live (MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, CERES and aerosol data). Data that a web page cannot read directly (NASA GISTEMP, MODIS NDVI and NPP, JPL MUR SST, MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll and the NSIDC Sea Ice Index) was downloaded once with our Python scripts and bundled, and is clearly labelled "Bundled sample data" in the app. The pipeline aggregates monthly values to one value per year for the chosen season, with strict rules for missing months, and then runs the tests:

- Mann-Kendall trend test, with the Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction as the main test and trend-free pre-whitening as a second check

- Sen's slope with a 95% confidence interval

- Pettitt change-point test, plus two-phase regression compared by BIC to see if a change sped up or slowed down

- Per-cell tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control for the map of change

- Agreement with an independent dataset (NOAA PSL station and reanalysis data, or ECMWF ERA5 for tapped points), with a break test on the difference that lowers confidence when the datasets disagree

- Season by season: the trend of every month, corrected for testing twelve months at once, and a year by month heatmap

- Compare two places: tests whether the gap between two regions is changing

- Explainable machine learning: a ridge regression shows which related variables help predict good and bad years, scored only on years it never saw, and always says that prediction is not cause

All statistics are written in TypeScript and unit-tested against the Python reference packages pymannkendall, SciPy and NumPy.

**Other features**

- "How sure are we?" panel that never rates a trend High when it is not significant or a second dataset contradicts it

- Live NASA GIBS satellite map (including MODIS NDVI, SMAP soil moisture and GPM rainfall layers) and a weather map page with NASA POWER panels and a historical analysis panel

- Search across NASA POWER parameters

- Charts with trend line and change point, anomaly bars, climate stripes, seasonal charts and a cross-variable "What changes together" view

- A farmer's story, quick-start questions (for example "Is Bangladesh getting hotter?", "Is winter haze over Dhaka getting worse?"), a first-visit tour, shareable links, PNG and CSV export, a one-page printable report and a Methods page

**Benefits and intended impact**

NASA publishes decades of Earth data, but a farmer in Rajshahi, a student or a local official cannot easily answer a simple question with it, such as "is monsoon rainfall here actually decreasing?" Simple charts can mislead, because climate series are noisy and datasets disagree, and most tools never say how sure they are. Our app gives scientists a fast, transparent analysis tool and gives everyone else a trustworthy plain-language answer. For example, it shows that Bangladesh's surface temperature (NASA GISTEMP) rose by about 1.40 °C over 1951 to 2025 with high confidence, while monsoon rainfall in Rajshahi shows no significant trend since 2001. We want communities in climate-vulnerable regions like Bangladesh to make decisions on farming, water and health from evidence rather than impressions.

**Tools, languages, hardware and software**

- Languages: TypeScript, Svelte, HTML and CSS for the app; Python for data download and reference tests

- Frameworks and libraries: SvelteKit (static build), Svelte 5, Vite, D3 for charts, MapLibre GL JS for maps, Tailwind CSS, bits-ui, Lucide icons, Turf.js, Vitest for tests, Prettier and ESLint

- Data access: NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS WMTS imagery, ORNL DAAC MODIS web service, NOAA PSL THREDDS, NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP, NSIDC, Open-Meteo APIs

- Base code: the open-source Open-Meteo Maps project (GPL-2.0), which we extended into a trend analysis tool

- Hardware: no special hardware. It runs in any modern browser on a phone or computer, and was tested in Chrome with phone emulation from 320 to 1366 px wide

**What makes it creative**

- It tells every result twice, once for scientists and once in plain language, from the same numbers

- It is honest about uncertainty: every answer has a confidence rating, checks a second dataset and detects when a dataset has a sudden break

- It combines classical trend statistics with explainable machine learning, and is clear that association and prediction are not cause

- It covers five Earth systems in one place, from Bangladesh rainfall and soil moisture to Bay of Bengal sea temperature and Arctic sea ice

**Factors we considered**

- Scientific honesty: noisy and autocorrelated data, testing many places or months at once, short records, satellite sensor changes and reanalysis disagreement (for example, MERRA-2 air temperature over Rajshahi disagrees with station data, so the app rates it Low confidence and uses NASA GISTEMP by default)

- Accessibility: mobile-first design, 44 px touch targets, AA colour contrast, colour-blind-safe charts, keyboard focus, dark mode and reduced motion

- Low connectivity and cost: no server, no login, results cached in the browser for a day

- Data access limits: SMAP and GRACE data files need an Earthdata login, so SMAP appears only as a map image layer and soil moisture comes from MERRA-2

- Transparency: open source code, a Methods page with every test and its reference, and clear labels for live versus bundled data
